correctness.rationale: Domination requires one vertex from every core–leaf pair. Adding an attacking selected leaf to a core attack cannot lower its surplus: if its leaf is newly reached, its +1 pays for the only possible new negative core; if the leaf is already reached, its support is already reached too. For a core attack I the surplus is twice the number of attacked A-pairs plus the signed number of newly reached external core positions. With no A, attacking all B positions in a mixed word exposes a negative C boundary, leaving precisely the two uniform sets. With a unique A, an internal B run exposes two distinct C positions; two B runs touching the ends of the tail expose A and two negative positions if their intervening C run has length at least two. Conversely a legal tail exposes at most two negatives when A is attacked, paid by +2; without A, it exposes at most one negative and the first un-attacked core on the B-chain from that boundary toward A gives +1. This includes n=3. Labelled counting uses n possible roots times (2n-2)+(n-3) distinct tails. Independently enumerating both subset sizes of the original vertex set and checking attacks against the definition for n=3,...,8 gave minimum counts all 2 and excess counts 12,28,50,78,112,152, with exact agreement per configuration.
residual_risks: The finite replay corroborates the all-n proof; it is not a substitute for it. No formal proof-assistant verification or attestation is inferred.

evidence: The thesis defines global secure as secure by the all-subsets neighborhood inequality and also dominating. Zeng et al. use the same condition and distinguish the Cockayne et al. usage.

The catalogued super-domination criterion requires an exclusive selected neighbor for each omitted vertex; the ordinary P3-convexity criterion limits the outside vertex to at most one selected neighbor.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Neither other condition is equivalent to all-subsets security. For example, the secure triangle-sunlet selection with cyclic word ABC fails super domination (the unselected B-leaf's only neighbor also sees the omitted C-core) and ordinary P3-convexity (the C-core sees multiple selected neighbors).

value.rationale: The first nonminimum size class is a natural next coefficient in a security spectrum, and the result explains exactly which selections attain it rather than tabulating a few cycles. The reduction of all-subsets attacks to charged core boundaries isolates the obstruction and applies uniformly to every cycle length. Value rests on that classification and coefficient, not on the known minimum.
residual_risks: No higher-excess spectrum or arbitrary one-leaf-corona classification is established.
